analogy.p: Think of energy as money moving between your wallet (the reacting chemicals) and your friend's wallet (the surroundings). In an exothermic reaction your wallet gives money to your friend, so the friend's wallet (the temperature of the surroundings) gets fuller. In an endothermic reaction you take money from your friend, so their wallet gets emptier. The total money never changes, just like energy is conserved. The analogy breaks down because money is counted in whole coins, whereas energy can be transferred in any amount.

bullets: **Energy is conserved:** the amount of energy in the universe at the end of a chemical reaction is the same as before the reaction.
**Exothermic:** energy is transferred **to** the surroundings; temperature of the surroundings **increases**.
**Endothermic:** energy is taken in **from** the surroundings; temperature of the surroundings **decreases**.
**Exothermic examples:** combustion, many oxidation reactions and neutralisation.
**Endothermic examples:** thermal decompositions and the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate.
**Everyday uses:** self-heating cans and hand warmers (exothermic); some sports injury packs (endothermic).
Exam skill: use **temperature change** evidence to classify a reaction and always refer to the **surroundings** in your answer.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This spec point asks you to understand that **energy is conserved in chemical reactions** and to describe **exothermic** reactions (which transfer energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings increases) and **endothermic** reactions (which take in energy from the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings decreases). You must be able to give **examples** of each, link them to everyday uses such as self-heating cans, hand warmers and some sports injury packs, and interpret temperature data to decide which type of reaction has happened. It is the foundation for reaction profiles, bond energy calculations and the required practical on temperature changes, so it is worth getting completely secure.

bullets: Energy is **not created or destroyed**, so energy lost by the reacting chemicals is **gained by the surroundings** (exothermic).
The **system** is the reacting chemicals; the **surroundings** are everything else, such as the solution, the beaker, the air and your hand.
We measure the energy change by measuring the **temperature change of the surroundings** (usually the water or solution).
If a reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, the **product molecules must have less energy than the reactants** by the amount transferred.
If a reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, the **products have more energy** than the reactants by the amount absorbed.
Link to other topics: this is the same conservation of energy principle used in Physics (energy stores and transfers).
Common phrase for marks: "**energy is transferred to / from the surroundings**"; avoid saying energy is "made" or "used up".
core.h: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions
core.p: The **law of conservation of energy** says that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another. In a chemical reaction the energy stored in chemical bonds can be transferred to the surroundings as thermal energy, or taken in from the surroundings. The **total energy** in the universe is the same at the end as at the start; it has simply moved. This idea is why we can talk about energy being "given out" or "taken in" without anything being made or lost.

bullets: Definition to learn: an exothermic reaction **transfers energy to the surroundings**, so the **temperature of the surroundings increases**.
Evidence: the **temperature rises** (e.g. from 20 °C to 28 °C) in a thermometer or the container feels **hot**.
**Combustion** of fuels such as methane: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, releasing a lot of energy as heat and light.
**Neutralisation:** acid + alkali → salt + water; the temperature of the mixture goes up.
**Oxidation:** many metals react with oxygen exothermically; the rusting of iron is exothermic but too slow to notice.
**Respiration** in cells is also exothermic; it releases energy, some of which keeps the body warm.
On an energy level diagram the **products are drawn lower** than the reactants.
core.p: An **exothermic reaction** is one that **transfers energy to the surroundings**. The surroundings get warmer, so a thermometer placed in the reaction mixture shows a **temperature rise**. Because the energy leaves the chemicals, the products have **less energy stored** than the reactants. Exothermic reactions are very common: all combustion (burning) reactions are exothermic, as are neutralisation reactions between an acid and an alkali and many oxidation reactions.

bullets: **Exothermic:** energy flows system → surroundings; ΔE of the system is **negative**; the temperature of the surroundings **rises**.
**Endothermic:** energy flows surroundings → system; ΔE is **positive**; the temperature of the surroundings **falls**.
Cold is **not** a thing that is made or transferred; an endothermic reaction **takes in energy**, so its surroundings lose energy and cool.
Energy transferred to the surroundings may spread to the air, so the **maximum** temperature is lower than it would be in a perfectly insulated container.
On a stored-energy bar chart the reactants bar is **higher** than the products bar for an exothermic reaction.
The size of the energy change depends on the **amounts** of reactants used, not only on the type of reaction.
The same ideas apply to **changes of state**, but the spec point here is about **chemical reactions**.
core.h: System, surroundings and the sign of the energy change
core.p: Chemists divide the world into the **system** (the atoms, ions and molecules that are reacting) and the **surroundings** (everything else: the solution, the container, the thermometer and the air). Energy is conserved, so **energy lost by the system = energy gained by the surroundings**, and the reverse. This is why the **temperature of the surroundings** is the evidence we measure: an exothermic reaction warms the surroundings, an endothermic one cools them. When writing answers, name the direction of transfer and the object it goes to or from, rather than saying that a reaction 'gives off heat' or 'makes cold'.

bullets: Definition to learn: an endothermic reaction **takes in energy from the surroundings**, so the **temperature of the surroundings decreases**.
Evidence: the **temperature falls** (e.g. from 22 °C to 15 °C) or the container feels **cold**.
**Thermal decomposition:** a compound breaks down when heated, e.g. calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide; energy must be **continually supplied**.
**Citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate** reaction makes the mixture cold, which can be shown with a thermometer.
**Photosynthesis** is endothermic: it takes in energy from sunlight to make glucose.
On an energy level diagram the **products are drawn higher** than the reactants.
An endothermic reaction can feel cold to the touch because **energy flows from your hand into the reaction**.
core.p: An **endothermic reaction** is one that **takes in energy from the surroundings**. The surroundings get cooler, so a thermometer shows a **temperature fall**. Because energy is absorbed, the products have **more energy stored** than the reactants. Endothermic reactions are much less common than exothermic ones in everyday life, but important examples include **thermal decompositions** and the reaction between **citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate**.

bullets: **Bond breaking** is **endothermic**: energy is **taken in** from the surroundings.
**Bond making** is **exothermic**: energy is **released** to the surroundings.
**Exothermic overall:** energy released making bonds is **greater** than the energy needed to break bonds.
**Endothermic overall:** energy needed to break bonds is **greater** than the energy released making bonds.
This explains the idea but the numerical bond energy calculations belong to the **Higher tier** reaction energy topic.
Link to other topics: the same idea explains why **combustion** gives out so much energy: strong bonds form in CO₂ and H₂O.
Never say "bond breaking releases energy"; this is one of the most common errors.
core.h: Where does the energy come from? Bonds and energy stores
core.p: Chemical reactions involve **breaking bonds in the reactants** and **making new bonds in the products**. Breaking bonds requires energy (it is **endothermic**) and making bonds releases energy (it is **exothermic**). Whether the whole reaction is exothermic or endothermic depends on which is larger. If more energy is released making the new bonds than is needed to break the old ones, the reaction is exothermic overall; if more energy is needed to break bonds than is released making new ones, it is endothermic overall.

bullets: **Combustion:** e.g. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O; used for heating, cooking and transport.
**Neutralisation:** e.g. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O; temperature rises by a few degrees in a simple experiment.
**Oxidation of iron** in hand warmers: iron powder reacts with oxygen in air, releasing heat.
**Reactive metal + acid:** magnesium + hydrochloric acid gets hot; a fast, strongly exothermic reaction.
**Respiration:** glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, with energy released for the body.
The **size** of the temperature rise depends on amounts and concentrations of the reactants, and how well the container is insulated.
In exam questions "burning" and "combustion" mean the same: both are **exothermic**.
core.h: Examples of exothermic reactions in detail
core.p: The main exothermic types you should be able to name are **combustion**, **oxidation** and **neutralisation**. In combustion, a fuel reacts with oxygen and releases large amounts of energy. In neutralisation, hydrogen ions from the acid react with hydroxide ions from the alkali to make water, warming the mixture. Metals reacting with acids (for example magnesium with hydrochloric acid) also release energy and the solution gets hot.

bullets: **Thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate:** CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂; needs a constant supply of energy.
**Thermal decomposition of copper carbonate:** green copper carbonate → black copper oxide + carbon dioxide; energy has to be supplied.
**Citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate:** produces carbon dioxide, and the temperature falls; used as a safe classroom demonstration.
**Photosynthesis:** carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, driven by light energy.
Endothermic reactions are used in **instant cold packs** for sports injuries.
If heating stops, a thermal decomposition **stops**, which shows that energy is being continually taken in.
Do not confuse **endothermic** with "slow" or "needs a spark"; the activation energy topic (reaction profiles) explains why even exothermic reactions may need a spark to start.
core.h: Examples of endothermic reactions in detail
core.p: The main endothermic reactions that you need to know are **thermal decompositions** and **citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate**. In thermal decomposition, a compound is broken down by heat; because energy is absorbed, you must keep heating for the reaction to continue. The citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate reaction is unusual because it happens at room temperature but still takes in energy from its surroundings, so the temperature drops.

bullets: **Self-heating can:** an exothermic reaction inside the can warms the food or drink without needing a stove.
**Hand warmers:** exothermic reaction (such as oxidation of iron) gives continuous warmth for some time.
**Instant cold packs:** an endothermic process absorbs energy from the injury and feels cold.
**Advantages of hand warmers/cans:** portable, no external heat source needed; **disadvantages:** may be single use, can get too hot, produce waste.
**Advantages of cold packs:** quick to use anywhere, no fridge needed; **disadvantages:** single use, only cool for a short time.
In evaluation questions mention **safety, cost, convenience, reusability and waste**.
Link to other topics: choosing the right reaction for a job is an example of applying science to real products.
core.h: Everyday uses of exothermic and endothermic reactions
core.p: Exothermic and endothermic reactions have practical uses. **Self-heating cans** (for example for hot drinks or food) and **hand warmers** use exothermic reactions to give out heat when needed. **Sports injury packs** can use endothermic reactions to cool an injury quickly when the pack is activated. In each case the design decision depends on whether you want to **transfer energy to** or **take energy from** the surroundings.

bullets: **Temperature change = final temperature − start temperature**: a positive value means exothermic; a negative value means endothermic.
Use the **maximum (or minimum) temperature reached** for a reaction mixture, not the temperature at the end of the experiment.
An **insulated cup with a lid** reduces energy loss, so the temperature change is closer to the true value.
**Stirring** makes sure the thermometer reads the temperature of the whole solution.
Measure the **same volumes and concentrations** each time if comparing reactions: these are **control variables**.
Use a **thermometer with suitable resolution** (e.g. 0.5 °C or 0.1 °C) and repeat to find a mean for reliability.
This links directly to the **required practical on temperature changes** (see the next spec point).
core.p: The simplest way to tell whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic is to measure the **temperature before and after** (or at regular intervals) with a thermometer or temperature probe. The change in temperature tells you the direction of energy transfer. To get reliable results the reaction is carried out in an **insulated container** (such as a polystyrene cup with a lid) to reduce energy transferred to the surroundings, and the mixture is **stirred** so that the temperature is uniform.

bullets: **Method:** measure a fixed volume of one solution (for example 25 cm³ acid) with a measuring cylinder into a polystyrene cup standing in a beaker for stability; record the **start temperature**.
Add the second reactant (for example 25 cm³ alkali), **replace the lid**, stir gently and record the temperature every 30 s (or use the **maximum or minimum** reading).
**ΔT = highest (or lowest) temperature − start temperature**; positive = exothermic, negative = endothermic.
**Control variables:** same volumes, same concentrations, same start temperature, same cup and lid, same stirring.
**Risks:** acids and alkalis can irritate skin and eyes (wear **eye protection**); mop up spills; some reactions, such as metal + acid, give off hydrogen so keep flames away.
**Improving accuracy:** insulate better, use a lid, use a thermometer with finer divisions (0.1 °C) and repeat to calculate a **mean**.
**Why the real ΔT is lower than the theory value:** some energy is lost to the surroundings of the cup and to the thermometer and cup themselves.
**Reliability:** repeat until results are close (concordant) and ignore any anomalies when calculating the mean.
core.h: Required practical: temperature changes in reacting solutions
core.p: AQA required practical 4 asks you to **investigate the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions**, for example acid + metal, acid + carbonate, neutralisation and displacement of metals. The reacting solution is the **surroundings** that you measure, so the aim is to detect the **energy transferred** as a temperature change. A **polystyrene cup** is used because it is a good **insulator**, and a lid reduces losses by evaporation and draughts. The independent variable might be the **type or concentration of reactant**; the dependent variable is the **temperature change (ΔT)**, and everything else must be kept the same.

bullets: The **steepest part** of the curve is where the reaction is fastest.
The **peak (or lowest point)** gives the largest temperature change; subtract the starting temperature.
The curve **levels off or returns** towards room temperature once the reaction has finished.
An **exothermic** graph goes **up then down**; an **endothermic** graph goes **down then up**.
If a question gives numbers, **quote them**: "temperature rose from 21 °C to 29 °C, a rise of 8 °C, so exothermic".
Axes: **time on the x-axis** with units (s or min), **temperature on the y-axis** in °C.
Link to other topics: the same type of graph appears in rate-of-reaction and cooling-curve questions.
core.p: Temperature–time graphs show how the temperature of the solution changes during a reaction. For an **exothermic** reaction the line rises above the starting temperature, reaches a maximum and then slowly falls as the mixture loses energy to the room. For an **endothermic** reaction the line drops below the start temperature, reaches a minimum and slowly climbs back. Both lines move back towards **room temperature** because energy is transferred between the surroundings and the room.

bullets: Forward exothermic means **reverse endothermic**, with the **same size** of energy change.
Hydrated copper(II) sulfate (blue) ⇌ anhydrous copper(II) sulfate (white) + water.
Heating the blue crystals is **endothermic**; adding water to the white powder is **exothermic** (it warms up).
This idea connects to **dynamic equilibrium** and **Le Chatelier's principle** (Higher tier) in Paper 2.
Energy is **conserved** here too: what is absorbed in one direction is released in the other.
The reaction profile for the reverse reaction is the **mirror image** of the forward one.
Exam use: if told a forward reaction is exothermic, state that the reverse is **endothermic** and transfers the **same amount** of energy.
core.p: Some reactions are **reversible**, meaning that products can react to re-form the reactants. If a reversible reaction is **exothermic in one direction** it is **endothermic in the opposite direction**, and the **same amount of energy** is transferred in each case. A common example is the thermal decomposition of hydrated copper sulfate: heating blue crystals drives off water (endothermic), and adding water to the white powder gives out energy (exothermic).

bullets: **Activation energy:** the **minimum energy** colliding particles need to react.
An exothermic reaction can still need heat or a spark to start, but **gives out more energy than it needs**.
On a reaction profile, **exothermic** has **products below reactants**; **endothermic** has **products above reactants**.
The **overall energy change** is the difference in height between reactants and products.
A catalyst **lowers the activation energy** but does not change the overall energy change.
Do not confuse **activation energy** (energy to start) with the **overall energy change** (net energy transferred).
Link to other topics: collision theory explains why raising the temperature increases the rate of both exothermic and endothermic reactions.
core.h: Linking ideas: reaction profiles and activation energy
core.p: Even exothermic reactions often need a small amount of energy to get started, called the **activation energy**. This is the minimum energy colliding particles must have to react. A match must be lit to start a fire, but once it is burning, the energy released keeps it going. Reaction profiles (the next spec point) show this on an energy diagram: reactants, the peak (activation energy) and products, with the overall energy change shown as the difference between reactants and products.

bullets: 1-mark: "What is an exothermic reaction?" → one that **transfers energy to the surroundings** (temperature of surroundings increases).
2-mark: "Explain why the temperature fell" → the reaction is **endothermic** (1) so it **takes in energy from the surroundings** (1).
Always say **surroundings**, not just "it gets hot"; the reaction mixture is part of what you measure.
For data questions, **calculate the temperature change** and state the sign.
Keep the words **exo**thermic = energy **ex**its; **endo**thermic = energy **en**ters.
If asked to give examples, name **specific reactions** such as combustion of methane, not just "burning things".
Do not write "the reaction makes heat"; write "the reaction **transfers energy to the surroundings**".
core.p: Questions on this spec point are usually short, but they test precise language. Marks are awarded for the **correct direction** of energy transfer (to or from the surroundings) and the **link with temperature**. Use the pattern: **type of reaction → energy direction → temperature change of the surroundings**. For evaluation or application questions give a reason linked to the use (e.g. why a hand warmer must use an exothermic reaction).

exam: **Definitions (1 to 2 marks):** use the exact wording: exothermic = transfers energy **to** the surroundings, temperature of surroundings **increases**; endothermic = takes in energy **from** the surroundings, temperature **decreases**.
**Classify from data (2 marks):** calculate the temperature change, state whether it is a rise or fall, then name exothermic or endothermic.
**Name examples (1 mark each):** exothermic: combustion, neutralisation, oxidation; endothermic: thermal decomposition, citric acid and sodium hydrogencarbonate.
**Everyday uses (2 marks):** name the product and say which type of reaction it relies on, e.g. a hand warmer uses an exothermic reaction to give out energy.
**Explain with energy conservation (3 marks):** energy is conserved, the products have less energy than the reactants, the difference is transferred to the surroundings.
**Bond explanation (3 to 4 marks):** compare energy needed to break bonds with energy released making bonds.
**Graph questions:** quote the start and maximum/minimum temperatures, and state the change with units.
**Practical questions:** mention a lid and insulation to reduce energy loss, stirring, and the same volumes as control variables.
**Evaluate uses (4 marks):** give one advantage and one disadvantage for each product, then a judgement.
**Command words:** "State" = brief fact; "Explain" = give a reason linked to energy; "Describe" = say what you would observe, e.g. the thermometer reading.
**Required practical (3 to 4 marks):** name the apparatus (polystyrene cup, lid, thermometer), the control variables (volumes, concentrations, start temperature) and calculate ΔT = max − start.

mistakes.r: Exothermic reactions **transfer energy to the surroundings**; the temperature **increases**.
mistakes.w: An exothermic reaction gets energy from the surroundings.

mistakes.r: Endothermic reactions **take in energy from the surroundings**, so the temperature of the surroundings **falls**.
mistakes.w: Endothermic means the temperature goes up because heat is added.

mistakes.r: **Breaking bonds takes in energy** (endothermic); **making bonds releases energy** (exothermic).
Energy is **conserved**; it is transferred from the surroundings to the chemicals.
mistakes.w: Energy is used up in endothermic reactions.

mistakes.r: Say the **surroundings** get hotter; the **products have less stored energy** than the reactants.
mistakes.w: The reaction gets hot, so the reactants are hotter than the products.

mistakes.r: Many exothermic reactions still need **activation energy** (e.g. a spark) to begin.
mistakes.w: Exothermic reactions do not need any energy to start.

mistakes.r: Thermal decomposition is **endothermic**; energy from the flame is **taken in** by the reaction.
mistakes.w: Thermal decomposition is exothermic because it uses a flame.

mistakes.r: **Temperature change = final − start temperature**; give the sign and units.
mistakes.w: The temperature change is the final temperature.

mistakes.r: Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings, so the surroundings cool down.

summary: You must understand that energy is conserved in chemical reactions, and describe exothermic reactions (energy transferred to the surroundings, temperature of surroundings rises) and endothermic reactions (energy taken in from the surroundings, temperature falls), giving examples and everyday uses. It matters because the idea underpins reaction profiles, bond energy calculations and the required practical on temperature changes.

terms.d: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Everything that is not the reacting chemicals, such as the solution, container and air.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another.
A reaction with oxygen that transfers energy to the surroundings; burning.
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen (or loses electrons).
The reaction of an acid with an alkali (or base) to form a salt and water.
A reaction in which a substance breaks down into simpler substances when heated.
Final temperature minus initial temperature, measured in °C.
A material such as polystyrene that reduces the transfer of energy to the surroundings.
The process of separating atoms joined by a bond; it takes in energy.
The process of forming new bonds; it releases energy.
The minimum amount of energy that colliding particles must have in order to react.
A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the original reactants.
A container in which an exothermic reaction heats the contents when it is activated.
The reacting chemicals; energy is transferred between the system and the surroundings.
Temperature change = final (max or min) temperature − start temperature; positive for exothermic, negative for endothermic.
An investigation in an insulated polystyrene cup measuring the temperature change of a reacting solution.

worked.q: In two experiments the temperature of the solution was measured. Experiment A: 20.0 °C to 27.5 °C. Experiment B: 21.0 °C to 14.5 °C. State whether each reaction is exothermic or endothermic, giving the temperature change. (4 marks)
steps: The temperature of the surroundings increased, so energy was transferred to the surroundings: exothermic.
The temperature of the surroundings decreased, so energy was taken in from the surroundings: endothermic.

worked.ans: The reaction is exothermic, so energy is transferred from the reacting chemicals to the surroundings. The products have less energy than the reactants, and energy is conserved, so the surroundings (the solution) gain that energy and the temperature rises.
worked.q: A student adds acid to alkali in a polystyrene cup and the temperature rises. Explain, using ideas about energy, why the temperature rises. (3 marks)
steps: Energy is conserved, so the products have less energy than the reactants.
The difference is transferred to the surroundings (the solution), so its temperature rises.

worked.ans: Self-heating cans use an exothermic reaction to heat food without a stove, which is convenient and portable, but they are single use and create waste. Cold packs use an endothermic reaction to take energy from an injury, which is quick and portable, but they are single use and only cool for a short time. Overall both are useful in emergencies but wasteful if used regularly.
worked.q: Evaluate the use of a self-heating can and an instant cold pack. (4 marks)
steps: Self-heating can: exothermic reaction transfers energy to the food or drink, so no stove is needed (advantage); but it is usually single use and adds waste (disadvantage).
Cold pack: endothermic reaction takes in energy from the injury so it cools quickly (advantage); but it is single use and only stays cold briefly (disadvantage).
Give a judgement, e.g. both are convenient for one-off use, but not suitable for repeated use because of waste.
